whatIsAac.lead: AAC stands for Augmentative and Alternative Communication — any method of communicating besides speech. It's for people who are nonspeaking, minimally verbal, or whose speech is hard for others to understand.
whatIsAac.vs.title: Augmentative vs. alternative
whatIsAac.vs.body: Augmentative means adding to speech (supporting the words someone already has). Alternative means communicating in place of speech. Many people use a mix, and their needs change over time — AAC meets them wherever they are.
whatIsAac.types.title: Types of AAC
whatIsAac.types.low: No-tech / low-tech: gestures, sign, or paper symbol boards and books.
whatIsAac.types.high: High-tech: apps and devices that speak aloud — like SayThrough — where you tap symbols and words to build messages.
whatIsAac.core.title: What are “core words”?
whatIsAac.core.body: A small set of about 200–400 core words (want, go, more, stop, help, I, you…) makes up roughly 80% of everyday speech. Good AAC keeps these high-frequency words in consistent, easy-to-reach places so they can be found by muscle memory. SayThrough's board is built around core vocabulary, with topic pages for the rest.
whatIsAac.speech.title: Does using AAC stop someone from talking?
whatIsAac.speech.body: No — research consistently shows the opposite. Offering AAC does not prevent speech; for many people it supports language development and can encourage more spoken words, not fewer. Read what the studies actually found.
whatIsAac.start.title: How do I get started?
whatIsAac.start.s1: Just start. You don't need a formal evaluation to explore AAC. Open a free app and let the person experience communicating.
whatIsAac.start.s2: Model it. Tap words yourself as you talk (“aided language stimulation”) so they see how messages are built.
whatIsAac.start.s3: Keep it available all the time — not just during “lessons.”
whatIsAac.start.s4: Loop in an SLP (speech-language pathologist) when you can, for personalized goals.
whatIsAac.try: Try it free. SayThrough is a free, open AAC app — no account, works offline. It's a no-cost way to start today.
quickStart.h1: Quick start: your first sentence in 5 minutes
quickStart.lead: No sign-up, no download, nothing to buy. Here's the fastest path from opening SayThrough to hearing it speak.
quickStart.s1.title: 1. Open the app
quickStart.s1.body: Open the app and tap “Try it first — nothing is saved” to jump straight in, or “Let's set up a voice” to create a saved profile (recommended if this is for someone who'll use it regularly). The first thing setup asks is the language — English, Español, Polski or Português. Picking one changes the board, the voice and the app's own words, and you can change it later in Settings.
quickStart.s2.title: 2. Build a message
quickStart.s2.body: You'll see a grid of color-coded words and picture symbols. Tap any word — like I, then want, then more — and each one is added to the message bar at the top.
quickStart.s2.b1: Made a mistake? Tap the ⌫ to remove the last word.
quickStart.s2.b2: Want a different form of a word? Press and hold it (e.g. go → going; in Spanish comer → como, in Polish woda → wodę).
quickStart.s2.b3: Need a word without a button? Open the Keys tab to type it — suggestions appear above the keyboard as you go, and it learns the words you use most.
quickStart.s3.title: 3. Speak it
quickStart.s3.body: Press the green ▶ Speak button and SayThrough reads the whole sentence aloud, highlighting each word as it's spoken. Tapping the sentence itself also speaks it.
quickStart.s3.tip: Tip: In Settings you can turn on “speak each word as you tap,” pick a voice, and adjust the speaking speed.
quickStart.s4.title: 4. Install it on your device
quickStart.s4.body: SayThrough is a web app you can install so it opens full-screen and works offline:
quickStart.s4.ios: iPad / iPhone (Safari): tap the Share icon → Add to Home Screen.
quickStart.s4.chrome: Chromebook / Chrome / Edge: click the Install icon in the address bar (or menu → Install SayThrough).

quickStart.next.b1: Create a profile and pick a starting vocabulary.
quickStart.next.b2: Customize the board — edit buttons, add your own photos, and link pages.
quickStart.next.b3: Set an access method (touch, dwell/hover, or switch scanning) in Settings.

compare.how.title: How can it be free?
compare.how.body: There is no company behind SayThrough to pay for. It is an open-source project built on symbol libraries that are themselves openly licensed — ARASAAC and Mulberry — and it runs in a browser, so there are no app-store fees, no servers to rent and no accounts to administer. Nothing is held back for a paid tier, because there is no paid tier and no plan to add one.
compare.try: You can try it in the next thirty seconds. No sign-up, no download, and nothing to uninstall if you decide against it.
tdSnap.h1: A free alternative to TD Snap
tdSnap.lead: TD Snap is a capable, well-supported AAC app that costs around $9.99 a month, or arrives bundled with a Tobii Dynavox device. SayThrough is free, open source and runs in a browser. Here is an honest account of where each one wins.
tdSnap.short: The short answer: if you already have TD Snap through funding or a device and it is working, stay. If you are paying out of pocket, waiting on a funding decision, or need AAC on twenty classroom Chromebooks tomorrow, SayThrough does the core job for nothing — and imports the boards you have already built.
tdSnap.them.title: What TD Snap does that SayThrough doesn't
tdSnap.them.body: This matters more than the price does. TD Snap is a mature commercial product with a clinical organisation behind it, and there are real things it offers that a free project does not.
tdSnap.them.b1: Professionally authored page sets. Core First, Motor Plan, Aphasia and PODD-style layouts, each developed and validated with clinicians. SayThrough ships one core-vocabulary system in three sizes; TD Snap ships a shelf of them.
tdSnap.them.b2: Dedicated device integration. Eye-gaze hardware, mounted speech-generating devices, environmental controls and partner-assisted scanning on Tobii Dynavox hardware. SayThrough runs on ordinary phones, tablets and laptops.
tdSnap.them.b3: Funding support. Tobii Dynavox will help build an insurance or education-authority funding claim, and that process often covers the device and the software together — in which case your out-of-pocket cost is not $9.99 a month at all.
tdSnap.them.b4: Paid support and training. A phone number, a support contract, structured training and implementation help. SayThrough has an issue tracker and an email address.
tdSnap.us.title: What SayThrough does that TD Snap doesn't
tdSnap.us.b1: It costs nothing, permanently. No subscription, no per-seat licence, no separate purchase for professionals. A school can put it on every device it owns without asking anyone for a budget.
tdSnap.us.b2: It runs on any device with a browser. Chromebook, Windows laptop, Android tablet, iPad, an old phone in a drawer. TD Snap is iPad and Windows.
tdSnap.us.b3: Four languages, each authored separately. English, Spanish, Polish and Brazilian Portuguese, with boards built for the language rather than translated from English — including gender agreement in Spanish and Portuguese and all seven cases in Polish.
tdSnap.us.b4: Open symbol libraries. ARASAAC and Mulberry, both openly licensed. Nothing you build is tied to a proprietary symbol set you could lose access to.
tdSnap.us.b5: It is open source. You can read the code, verify the privacy claims rather than trust them, fork it, or keep it running yourself if the project ever stops. No vendor can discontinue it out from under you.
tdSnap.table.title: Side by side
tdSnap.move.title: Moving your boards across
tdSnap.move.body: SayThrough reads and writes Open Board Format (.obf and .obz), the open interchange standard for AAC boards. Where you can export a vocabulary in that format, SayThrough will import it — buttons, labels, the links between pages, and the layout.
tdSnap.move.caveat: Two honest caveats. Proprietary symbols such as PCS cannot travel with the file, because their licence does not permit it — imported buttons keep their words and are re-matched to the nearest ARASAAC symbol, which you can change. And anything with no equivalent in the format, such as vendor-specific action buttons, arrives as a plain button. Check a copy before you rely on it.
tdSnap.who.title: Who should switch, and who shouldn't
tdSnap.who.stay: Stay with TD Snap if it is funded and working, if the user relies on eye gaze or a dedicated speech-generating device, if your team is trained on Core First or PODD and the motor plan is established, or if you need someone contractually obliged to answer the phone. Do not disrupt a communication system that works in order to save money.
tdSnap.who.switch: Try SayThrough if you are paying for TD Snap yourself, if you are waiting on a funding decision and need something in the meantime, if you need AAC across a classroom or a whole school, if you need a language TD Snap does not author boards for, or if you want a free second system on a device the user already carries. It costs nothing to find out, and it imports what you have built.
tdSnap.try: Nothing to lose. SayThrough opens in a browser with no sign-up and no download — you can test it against your current board in a few minutes.
proloquo.lead: Proloquo2Go is the best-known AAC app on iOS and costs around $249 as a one-time purchase. SayThrough is free, open source, and runs in any browser. Here is where each one earns its place.
proloquo.short: The short answer: Proloquo2Go is a polished, deeply researched iPad app, and $249 buys it outright with no subscription. SayThrough costs nothing and runs everywhere, including the Chromebook or Android tablet a school already owns. If $249 is not a problem and you are on iPad, Proloquo2Go is excellent. If it is a problem, you are not giving up much.
proloquo.them.title: What Proloquo2Go does that SayThrough doesn't
proloquo.them.body: Proloquo2Go has had more than a decade of iteration and a research programme behind its vocabulary. That shows.
proloquo.them.b1: A developmentally sequenced vocabulary. Its core vocabulary was built and refined over years, with a clear growth path from a handful of buttons to a full language system. SayThrough's three board sizes are a candidate set still awaiting formal clinical review.
proloquo.them.b2: Deep iOS integration. Native Apple voices, Switch Control, Voice Control, iCloud backup, and everything else an app built for a single platform can take for granted.
proloquo.them.b3: A large support ecosystem. Books, courses, video channels, consultants and school-district familiarity. Ask an SLP for help with Proloquo2Go and they will have seen it before.
proloquo.them.b4: Polish that only time buys. Progressive language levels, detailed pronunciation editing, and an editor that has had a great many hours put into it.
proloquo.us.title: What SayThrough does that Proloquo2Go doesn't
proloquo.us.b1: It costs nothing. $249 is a real barrier for a family testing whether AAC is right for their child, and an impossible one for a classroom of ten.
proloquo.us.b2: It is not iOS-only. Chromebooks dominate schools and Android dominates most of the world. Proloquo2Go runs on neither.
proloquo.us.b3: Four separately authored languages — including Polish, which very few AAC apps support properly, with the case system and speaker gender the language actually requires.
proloquo.us.b4: Open symbols and an open file format. Boards export to .obf/.obz and can be taken elsewhere. Nothing you build is trapped.
proloquo.us.b5: It is auditable. The code is public, so the privacy claim — that nothing anyone types or says leaves the device — can be checked rather than believed.
proloquo.table.title: Side by side
proloquo.move.title: Moving your boards across
proloquo.move.body: SayThrough imports and exports Open Board Format (.obf / .obz). Wherever you can get an Open Board Format export out of your current app, SayThrough will read it — buttons, labels, page links and layout.
proloquo.move.caveat: The honest caveat is symbols: proprietary sets such as SymbolStix and PCS are licensed and cannot travel with the file. Imported buttons keep their words and are matched to the closest ARASAAC symbol, which you can swap. Always check a copy before depending on it.
proloquo.who.title: Who should switch, and who shouldn't
proloquo.who.stay: Stay with Proloquo2Go if you have already bought it, if the user has an established motor plan in its vocabulary, if you are committed to iPad, or if your support team knows that app and not this one. A paid-for, working AAC system is worth far more than the money you would save.
proloquo.who.switch: Try SayThrough if $249 is the reason you have not started, if you need it on a Chromebook or Android device, if you need Spanish, Polish or Brazilian Portuguese boards authored in the language, if you need the same system across a whole class, or if you want a free backup that can live on every device the family owns.
proloquo.try: It is free to find out. Open SayThrough in a browser, build a sentence, and judge it for yourself — there is no purchase to regret.
coreWords.h1: Core words: the list, and why it matters
coreWords.lead: A few hundred words do most of the work in everyday speech. Choosing them well — and putting them somewhere they never move — is the single biggest decision in an AAC system. Here is the core vocabulary SayThrough ships, and the reasoning behind it.
coreWords.what.title: What are core words?
coreWords.what.body: Core words are the high-frequency words that work in almost any situation: want, go, more, stop, help, I, you, not, it, that. Studies of everyday language have consistently found that a set of roughly 200–400 of them accounts for around 80% of what people actually say. Their opposite is fringe vocabulary — nouns like banana, trampoline or dinosaur — which is enormous, deeply personal, and useful only in the one situation it names.
coreWords.why.title: Why core words come first
coreWords.why.body: It is tempting to fill a board with photographs of favourite foods and toys, because those are easy to make and easy to test. Core vocabulary is the better investment, for three reasons:
coreWords.why.b1: It goes further. More works at dinner, in the park, in the bath and in an argument about a film. Banana works at breakfast.
coreWords.why.b2: It builds sentences. Nouns alone produce labelling. Verbs, pronouns and little words produce I want that, go outside, stop it, not now — real language, with grammar in it.
coreWords.why.b3: It rewards motor learning. Because core words are used constantly and never move, their location becomes automatic — found by muscle memory rather than searched for. That is why SayThrough never reflows a board: raising the vocabulary level reveals words in place instead of rearranging them.
coreWords.list.title: The SayThrough core word list
coreWords.list.body: Below is the actual core vocabulary in SayThrough's expanded board — {{coreWordTotal}} core words in total: the always-on words that stay on screen wherever you are, plus the core pages behind them. This list is generated from the same data the app boots from, so it cannot drift from what you will see in the product.
coreWords.list.key: Colours follow the Fitzgerald Key, the convention most AAC systems share: yellow pronouns, green verbs, blue question words, orange little words, purple describing words, pink social words.
coreWords.sizes.title: Three sizes, one motor plan
coreWords.sizes.body: The same vocabulary is authored at three grid sizes — a 26-word starter board, a 196-word standard board, and the 513-word expanded board whose core is listed above. You choose the size once, at setup, because changing a grid moves every word and destroys the motor plan. Within a size, the vocabulary level controls which words are visible: raising it reveals more words exactly where they were always going to be, so nothing a learner already knows ever moves.
coreWords.teach.title: How to start with core words
coreWords.teach.s1: Pick five, not fifty. More, go, stop, want and help will carry a week comfortably.
coreWords.teach.s2: Model them yourself. Tap the words on the device as you speak. This is called aided language stimulation, and it is the single most effective thing a communication partner does.
coreWords.teach.s3: Use them in real moments. Core words earn their keep during snacks, transitions and play — not in a drill at a table.
coreWords.teach.s4: Don't test. Resist asking “what's this?”. Comment, offer a choice, and wait. Communication is not an exam.
coreWords.try: See the board for yourself. SayThrough opens in a browser with this vocabulary already loaded — free, and with no account.
aacSpeech.h1: Does using AAC stop a child from talking?
aacSpeech.lead: This is the question almost every parent asks first, and the worry behind it is entirely reasonable. The research answer has been consistent for more than twenty years, and it is not the one most people expect.
aacSpeech.short: No. Introducing AAC does not prevent or delay speech. Across the published research the effect on speech production is neutral to positive — most studies that measure it find gains, not losses — and no study has found that AAC suppressed speech development.
aacSpeech.research.title: What the research found
aacSpeech.research.body: The concern was studied directly, and repeatedly, because clinicians kept meeting it:
aacSpeech.research.b1: A systematic review by Millar, Light and Schlosser (2006) examined studies of AAC intervention and speech production. The large majority of participants showed gains in speech; none showed a decrease attributable to AAC.
aacSpeech.research.b2: Schlosser and Wendt (2008) reviewed AAC intervention with children with autism and reached the same conclusion — no evidence of speech being inhibited, with modest gains common.
aacSpeech.research.b3: Romski and Sevcik's work on augmented language input found that children given AAC alongside spoken language made greater gains in spoken vocabulary than those given spoken language alone.
aacSpeech.research.close: Different populations, different methods, the same direction of result. This is about as settled as questions in this field get.
aacSpeech.why.title: Why it works that way
aacSpeech.why.body: Speech is hard. Communication is the goal, and speech is only one route to it. When someone finally has a route that works, several things follow at once: the pressure comes off, communication attempts go up, and every attempt is now paired with a spoken model — the device says the word, an adult repeats it, and the person hears the target while succeeding at the message. AAC also makes the point of language obvious. Someone who has never successfully asked for anything has very little reason to practise asking.
aacSpeech.wait.title: Is my child too young?
aacSpeech.wait.body: There is no minimum age and no list of prerequisite skills. The old idea that a child must first demonstrate cause and effect, or reach a certain mental age, or show “readiness”, has been abandoned — it kept the children who needed communication most waiting the longest. Toddlers use AAC successfully. If a child is old enough to want something, they are old enough to have a way to ask for it.
aacSpeech.old.title: Is my child too old?
aacSpeech.old.body: No. AAC is introduced successfully to teenagers and adults, including people who used speech and lost it after a stroke, an injury, or a progressive condition. What changes with age is the vocabulary and the way the system looks — not whether it can work.
aacSpeech.do.title: What to do about it
aacSpeech.do.s1: Start now. You do not need an evaluation to let someone try a free app. Waiting has a cost; trying does not.
aacSpeech.do.s2: Model without demanding. Tap words as you talk, and do not require the device to be used before granting a request.
aacSpeech.do.s3: Keep speech welcome. AAC does not replace whatever speech someone has — accept every word, sound, sign and gesture. It is all communication.
aacSpeech.sources.title: Sources
aacSpeech.sources.s1: Millar, D. C., Light, J. C., & Schlosser, R. W. (2006). The impact of augmentative and alternative communication intervention on the speech production of individuals with developmental disabilities: a research review. Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research, 49(2), 248–264.
aacSpeech.sources.s2: Schlosser, R. W., & Wendt, O. (2008). Effects of augmentative and alternative communication intervention on speech production in children with autism: a systematic review. American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology, 17(3), 212–230.
aacSpeech.sources.s3: Romski, M., & Sevcik, R. A. (2005). Augmentative communication and early intervention: myths and realities. Infants & Young Children, 18(3), 174–185.
aacSpeech.notAdvice: This page summarises published research for general information. It is not clinical advice — a speech-language pathologist who knows the person can help turn it into a plan.
aacSpeech.try: You can start today. SayThrough is free and opens in a browser, so trying AAC costs nothing but the next five minutes.
access.h1: Access methods: touch, dwell and switch scanning
access.lead: An AAC system is only as good as someone's ability to operate it. If touching a small target is hard, unreliable or exhausting, the answer is not a simpler vocabulary — it is a different access method. SayThrough has three built in, all free, on every device.
access.touch.title: Direct touch
access.touch.body: The default, and the fastest wherever it works: tap a button and the word is added. If touch is nearly working but not quite, adjust before abandoning it — a smaller grid size gives bigger targets, and the board can be set to speak a word the moment it is selected. Accuracy problems are very often target-size problems in disguise.
access.dwell.title: Dwell (hover to select)
access.dwell.body: With dwell, holding a pointer still over a button for a set time selects it — no click, no tap. This suits anyone driving a pointer with a head mouse, a joystick, a trackball or eye-gaze hardware, and anyone for whom the click itself is the difficult part rather than the aiming.
access.dwell.b1: Set the dwell time to the person, not to an average. Too short and the board fires words while they are still looking; too long and every sentence becomes work.
access.dwell.b2: Watch for accidental selections along the way. If words are picked up while moving across the board, lengthen the dwell time before rearranging anything.
access.scan.title: Switch scanning
access.scan.body: Scanning moves a highlight through the board on its own, and the person presses a switch when it reaches what they want. Any switch that presents itself as a key press will work — a button switch on a USB or Bluetooth interface, a keyboard key, a tablet's accessibility switch. It is the access method of last resort in the best sense: when almost nothing else is voluntary and repeatable, one reliable movement is enough to talk.
access.scan.b1: Row–column scanning steps through rows first, then the cells within the chosen row. That is far fewer steps than scanning every cell in turn, and it is the standard choice on a board of any size.
access.scan.b2: Automatic or step scanning. Automatic advances on a timer and the switch selects; step advances on each switch press, with a second switch or a dwell to select. Step is slower but removes all timing pressure.
access.scan.b3: Scan speed is the whole game. Set it slow enough that a correct press is achievable every single time, then speed up only as reliability allows.
access.scan.tip: Allow more time than feels comfortable. The gap between the highlight arriving and the switch press has to cover seeing it, deciding, and moving — and for many people that chain is far longer than their understanding. A scan that is slightly too fast produces constant errors and looks exactly like a comprehension problem when it is a timing problem.
access.choose.title: Choosing between them
access.choose.body: Start with the most direct method the person can use reliably, because it is always the fastest — direct touch beats dwell, and dwell beats scanning, by a wide margin. Move down that list only when the method above it genuinely is not working, and be willing to move back up as motor skills change. An occupational therapist, or an SLP with AAC experience, is worth a great deal here; the hardware question is often theirs to answer rather than yours.
access.setup.title: Setting it up in SayThrough
access.setup.s2: Choose touch, dwell or scanning, then set the timing — dwell time, or scan speed and scanning pattern.
access.setup.s3: Test it on a whole message, not a single button. What you are checking is whether a complete sentence is achievable without exhaustion.
access.setup.close: All three methods are included at no cost and on every device, because an access method is not a premium feature — it is the difference between an app someone can use and an app they cannot.
access.try: Try the access settings. They are available from the first moment, with no profile and no account required.
install.h1: Installing SayThrough on iPad, Chromebook and Android
install.lead: SayThrough is a web app, so there is nothing to download from an app store and no licence to manage. Installing it simply means adding it to the home screen — after which it opens full-screen, launches like any other app, and works with no internet at all.
install.why: Why bother installing? An installed copy opens without browser chrome, starts faster, keeps working offline, and — most importantly — survives a bad or absent network. Communication should never depend on Wi-Fi.
install.ios.title: iPad and iPhone (Safari)
install.ios.s1: Open saythrough.com/app/ in Safari. It has to be Safari — on iOS, other browsers cannot install web apps.
install.ios.s2: Tap the Share button (the square with an arrow coming out of it).
install.ios.s3: Scroll down, tap Add to Home Screen, then Add.
install.ios.note: The icon appears on the home screen and opens full-screen with no address bar. If you use Guided Access to lock a child into a single app, it behaves exactly as an App Store app does.
install.chrome.title: Chromebook, Chrome and Edge
install.chrome.s2: Click the install icon in the address bar — a small screen with a downward arrow — or open the browser menu and choose Install SayThrough.
install.chrome.s3: Confirm. It appears in the launcher and can be pinned to the shelf.
install.chrome.note: On a managed Chromebook, an administrator can also push SayThrough to every device as a web app through the Google Admin console, so students find it already installed. There are no licences to buy or assign.
install.android.title: Android
install.android.s2: Open the browser menu and choose Install app or Add to Home screen.
install.schools.title: Notes for schools and IT
install.schools.body: SayThrough was built with school networks in mind, since they are usually the most restricted environment it has to run in.
install.schools.b1: One domain to allow: saythrough.com. The app, its symbols and its voices are all served from that one origin — there are no third-party CDNs, trackers or font services to allow separately.
install.schools.b2: No accounts, no logins, no per-seat licences. Nothing to provision at the start of the year and nothing to deprovision at the end of it.
install.schools.b3: No student data leaves the device. Profiles, boards and message history stay in the browser's local storage. Nothing anyone types or says is ever transmitted.
install.offline.title: Using it offline
install.offline.body: Once installed and opened at least once, SayThrough runs with no connection at all. The app, the boards and the symbols used by the active page set are cached on the device. If you need the entire symbol library available offline — for a trip, or a building with no signal — there is an optional full symbol pack in Settings that downloads all of it in one go.
install.try: Install it now. Open the app, then follow the steps above for your device — it takes about twenty seconds.
